contribution: Physics builds models and tests them with measurements, and the sizes of objects are understood as powers of ten: a size is written in the form $a\cdot10^{n}$, the ratio of sizes is found by dividing the larger size by the smaller, and each step of a power of ten is a tenfold size. With the zoom simulation the student compares an atom and its nucleus, and the Solar System and the Milky Way, and the theory brings together the structure of matter (molecule–atom–nucleus–nucleon–quark), Earth's place in the structures of the universe, the types of astronomical objects and the four fundamental interactions qualitatively.
learn: You can describe the structure of matter from molecules to quarks and Earth's place in the structures of the universe.
You can write a size in scientific notation and compare sizes using orders of magnitude.
You recognise the four fundamental interactions and can link a phenomenon to each.
prior: Powers from lower secondary school mathematics, for example $10^{3} = 1000$ and $10^{-2} = 0.01$
The units of length: metre, millimetre and kilometre

activities.text: Physics studies the smallest and the largest structures we know with the same principles. The size of a proton is about $1.7\cdot10^{-15}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of the observable universe about $8.8\cdot10^{26}\,\text{m}$. Neither can be seen with the naked eye or measured with a metre rule, and yet their sizes are known.
activities.question: What is matter made of, what larger structures is Earth a part of, and how many powers of ten are there between the smallest and the largest size?

choices.feedback: A negative exponent does not make the number negative. It means division: $10^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{10^{3}} = \dfrac{1}{1000}$.
Correct: $10^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{1000} = 0.001$. The exponent $-3$ moves the decimal point three places to the left, and these steps are the basis of powers of ten.
This has one zero too many: $0.0001 = 10^{-4}$. In $10^{-3}$ there are three decimal places after the point, and the last of them is the one: $0.001$.
This is $3\cdot10^{-2}$, not $10^{-3}$. The exponent tells in which decimal place the one is; it does not multiply the number by three.

activities.title: Prediction 1: an atom and its nucleus
activities.prompt: The diameter of a hydrogen atom is about $1.1\cdot10^{-10}\,\text{m}$. At the centre of the atom is the nucleus, which in hydrogen is a single proton. By how many orders of magnitude is the atom larger than its nucleus?

choices.text: About one order of magnitude: the nucleus fills a large part of the atom, as pictures of atoms often seem to show.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model, the order of magnitude of a hydrogen atom is $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$ and that of a proton $10^{-15}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is five orders of magnitude. In pictures of atoms the nucleus is deliberately drawn far too large so that it can be seen: in the right proportion it would be an invisible dot at the centre of the atom.

The values of the model support this: the order of magnitude of a hydrogen atom is $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$ and that of a proton $10^{-15}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is $-10-(-15) = 5$. So the atom is tens of thousands of times larger than its nucleus: if the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus at its centre would be the size of a pea.

Ten orders of magnitude is the difference between an atom and a person. In the values of the model, the nucleus is of the order $10^{-15}\,\text{m}$ and the atom $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is five orders of magnitude: huge, but smaller than the difference between an atom and a person.

choices.text: None, because an atom and its nucleus are the same thing.
choices.feedback: An atom and a nucleus are not the same thing: the nucleus is only the central part of the atom, and the atom also includes the electrons moving around the nucleus. In the values of the model, the atom is five orders of magnitude larger than its nucleus.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the Solar System and the Milky Way
activities.prompt: The planets of the Solar System orbit the Sun out to the orbit of Neptune. The Sun is one of the stars of the Milky Way. By how many orders of magnitude is the Milky Way larger than the region of the planets of the Solar System?

choices.text: About two orders of magnitude: the Solar System fills a considerable part of the Milky Way.
choices.feedback: In the values of the model, the order of magnitude of the orbit of Neptune is $10^{13}\,\text{m}$ and that of the Milky Way $10^{21}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is eight orders of magnitude. In the Milky Way the Solar System is smaller than a grain of sand on a football pitch, and the galaxy also has hundreds of billions of other stars.

In the values of the model the difference is eight orders of magnitude: the orbit of Neptune is of the order $10^{13}\,\text{m}$ and the Milky Way $10^{21}\,\text{m}$. Four orders of magnitude is only the order of the distance between the orbit of Neptune and the nearest star, and the Milky Way is much larger still.

The values of the model support this: the orbit of Neptune is of the order $10^{13}\,\text{m}$ and the Milky Way $10^{21}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is $21-13 = 8$. The Milky Way is about a hundred million times larger than the region of the planets.

Sixteen orders of magnitude would mean a $10^{16}$-fold difference. In the values of the model the difference is eight orders of magnitude: the orbit of Neptune is of the order $10^{13}\,\text{m}$ and the Milky Way $10^{21}\,\text{m}$. Eight tenfold steps already make a hundred-million-fold difference.

activities.text: Zoom from the Planck length to the observable universe. All the objects that fit in the picture are shown at the same time in the right proportions of size, and the bar at the bottom shows how long a power of ten of metres is on this scale.
activities.howto: Choose an object from the menu *Go to object*, and the picture slides to the scale where that object is the nearest in size. The buttons *Zoom in by a factor of $10$* and *Zoom out by a factor of $10$* change the width of the view to a tenth or ten times as much. The objects stand side by side by size: the smallest on the left, and an object larger than the picture is cut off at the edge of the picture. An object a few pixels in size is a dot, and a line points from it to its name. You can also drag the *Width of the view* slider, drag the picture sideways or click a place on the map. *Start* zooms automatically, and *Direction* and *Speed* choose the direction and the pace. The dots on the map are objects, and the light band shows which sizes fit in the picture now.
activities.model: The sizes are rounded order-of-magnitude values, not exact measurement results. The values are rounded model values from the literature: the Planck length is a quantity calculated from constants of nature, the astronomical unit $1\,\text{AU}$ and the light-year are agreed definitions, the sizes of the proton and the atom are based on scattering experiments and the quantum mechanical model, the size of the Milky Way is an estimate (about $10^{5}$ light-years, uncertainty tens of percent) and the diameter of the universe is inferred from observations with a cosmological model. The sizes of a hair, a red blood cell, an ant, a coin, a ball, a whale and a person are typical values, and individuals vary. The size of a quark is an upper limit obtained from observations. The size of a water molecule is a typical value, the diameter of a neutron star is a typical value based on observations and models (about $20$–$25\,\text{km}$), and for the black hole Sgr A* at the centre of the Milky Way the size drawn is the diameter of its event horizon, calculated from its mass (about $4.3$ million solar masses). A black hole is not a solid sphere: the boundary drawn is the event horizon, and the gas glowing around it and the radiation beams of a neutron star are illustrations. The sizes of nuclei, atoms and the Moon and Jupiter are rounded table values. The drawings are illustrations. At the Planck length the grid is only a symbol, because there are no observations of the structure of length. The electron cloud of a hydrogen atom is a probability picture, and its nucleus is drawn too large. On the orbits, stars and planets are enlarged dots, and the size marked for the orbits is their radius, although the picture is drawn by diameter. The Milky Way and the universe are artists' impressions.
activities.calc: The width of the view $W$ corresponds to $560$ pixels in the picture. An object of size $d$ is drawn in the picture with a width of $\dfrac{d}{W}\cdot560$ pixels. For example, when the width of the view is $10^{-9}\,\text{m}$, a hydrogen atom is $\dfrac{1.1\cdot10^{-10}\,\text{m}}{10^{-9}\,\text{m}}\cdot560 \approx 62$ pixels wide. An object is visible when its size is about $\dfrac{1}{1000}$–$3$ times the width of the view: an object under $4$ pixels is a dot, and an object larger than the picture is cut off at the edge. The number on the slider is the exponent of the width: the number $-9$ means a width of $10^{-9}\,\text{m}$. When the view zooms out tenfold, all objects shrink to a tenth.

activities.title: Experiment 1: the steps of matter
activities.intro: Test prediction 1. In the initial state the nearest object in size is the water molecule. Press *Record measurement*. Then use the *Go to object* menu to select a hydrogen atom, a proton and a quark in turn, and record a row for each. The $n$ in the table gives the order of magnitude of the nearest object: the size of the object is about $10^{n}\,\text{m}$. The value for the quark is an upper limit.

question.prompt: Use the rows of the hydrogen atom and the proton in the table. By how many orders of magnitude is the hydrogen atom larger than its nucleus?
hints: From the table you get the exponent $n$ of the order of magnitude of both objects. The nucleus of a hydrogen atom is a single proton.

Calculate how many steps of powers of ten there are from the order of magnitude of the proton to that of the hydrogen atom. The number of steps is the difference of the exponents, the smaller subtracted from the larger.
If the row of the hydrogen atom has $n = -10$ and the row of the proton $n = -15$, the number of steps is $-10 - (-15)$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the ratio of the sizes, that is, how many times larger the atom is. What was asked is the number of steps of powers of ten, that is, the difference of the exponents.
The magnitude is right but the sign is not. The atom is larger than its nucleus, so the difference is calculated as the smaller subtracted from the larger: $-10 - (-15) = 5$.
You added the exponents. The difference of orders of magnitude is the difference of the exponents: $-10 - (-15) = -10 + 15 = 5$.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the table, in the row of the hydrogen atom $n_\text{atom} = -10$ and in the row of the proton, that is, the nucleus of the hydrogen atom, $n_\text{proton} = -15$

**Find:** the difference of the orders of magnitude, that is, the number of steps of powers of ten between the atom and its nucleus

**Principle:** The exponent $n$ tells which power of ten the size is in. Each step from one power of ten to the next is a tenfold size, and the number of steps is the difference of the exponents, the smaller subtracted from the larger.

**Formula:** $\text{steps} = n_\text{atom} - n_\text{proton}$

**Conversions:** Not needed: the exponents are numbers without a unit.

**Substitution:** $\text{steps} = -10 - (-15) = -10 + 15 = 5$

**Answer:** $5$ orders of magnitude; the number is an integer, because $n$ is rounded to a whole power of ten.

**Reasonableness:** Five steps mean about $10^{5}$, that is, a hundred-thousandfold size. The exact ratio is $1.1\cdot10^{-10}\,\text{m} : 1.7\cdot10^{-15}\,\text{m} \approx 6.5\cdot10^{4}$, which is close to that. The difference is much smaller than the ten orders of magnitude between an atom and a person.

activities.title: Experiment 2: Earth's address
activities.intro: Test prediction 2. In the initial state the nearest object in size is Earth. Record a row. Then use the *Go to object* menu to select the Sun, the radius of Neptune's orbit and the Milky Way in turn, and record a row for each. If you like, continue all the way to the observable universe.

question.prompt: The objects in the table are in order of size. Which statement correctly describes how they are related?

choices.text: Earth orbits the Sun, the Sun is one of the stars of the Milky Way, and the Milky Way is one of the many galaxies of the observable universe.
choices.feedback: Correct. The structures are nested: Earth is in the Solar System, the Solar System in the Milky Way and the Milky Way in the observable universe. According to the table, each next structure is several orders of magnitude larger than the previous one: from the orbit of Neptune to the Milky Way is eight orders of magnitude.

choices.text: The Milky Way is the outermost part of the Solar System, where there are other stars.
choices.feedback: The order is the other way round: the Solar System is inside the Milky Way, not the Milky Way inside the Solar System. The Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars, and the Sun is one of them. According to the table, the Milky Way is about eight orders of magnitude larger than the region of the planets of the Solar System.

choices.text: The Milky Way is the same thing as the observable universe, because all the stars and galaxies we see are in the Milky Way.
choices.feedback: The individual stars visible to the naked eye are in the Milky Way, but the Milky Way is only one galaxy. For example, the Andromeda Galaxy is outside the Milky Way, and the observable universe is about six orders of magnitude larger than the Milky Way.

choices.text: The Sun is the centre of the Milky Way, around which the other stars of the galaxy orbit.
choices.feedback: The Sun is one ordinary star about 26 000 light-years from the centre of the Milky Way. The stars of the Milky Way, including the Sun, orbit the centre of the galaxy, and at the centre there is a black hole.

activities.title: Optional experiment: where is the midpoint of the sizes?
activities.intro: In the initial state the nearest object in size is the observable universe. Record a row. Then use the *Go to object* menu to select the Planck length and record a second row. In the question, calculate the midpoint between these two. Then zoom to the object in the model whose size is closest to this midpoint, and record a third row: the simulation shows which object is in the middle. Guess first: is the human in the middle of the sizes?

question.prompt: Calculate the mean of the $n$ values of the smallest and the largest object, that is, the midpoint on the axis of orders of magnitude. Then zoom to it, record the third row and answer: what is the $n$ of the nearest object in the simulation?
hints: Choose the rows of the Planck length and the universe in the table and read their $n$ values.
The midpoint is the mean of two numbers, $n_\text{mid} = \dfrac{n_\text{min} + n_\text{max}}{2}$. Use the exponents, not the sizes in metres.
If $n_\text{min} = -35$ and $n_\text{max} = 27$, then $n_\text{mid} = \dfrac{-35 + 27}{2}$. Then find the object whose size is about $10^{-4}\,\text{m}$, and record the third row.

mistakes.feedback: This is the distance from the midpoint to either end, that is, how many orders of magnitude there are from the midpoint to the Planck length. What was asked is the position of the midpoint, which is found as a mean: $\dfrac{-35 + 27}{2}$.
You took the mean of the sizes in metres, which gives roughly half the size of the universe. With orders of magnitude, the midpoint is calculated as the mean of the exponents.

question.solution:
**Given:** from the table, in the row of the Planck length $n_\text{min} = -35$ and in the row of the universe $n_\text{max} = 27$

**Find:** the exponent of the midpoint $n_\text{mid}$

**Principle:** The sizes are in many different powers of ten, so "in the middle" means the same number of orders of magnitude from each end. It is the mean of the exponents, not the mean of the sizes in metres.

**Formula:** $n_\text{mid} = \dfrac{n_\text{min} + n_\text{max}}{2}$

**Conversions:** Not needed: the exponents are numbers without a unit.

**Substitution:** $n_\text{mid} = \dfrac{-35 + 27}{2} = \dfrac{-8}{2} = -4$

**Answer:** $-4$, that is, a size of about $10^{-4}\,\text{m}$; an integer, because the exponents are integers. When you zoom here, the nearest object in the simulation is a hair, whose $n = -4$: the calculated midpoint and the object in the simulation agree.

**Reasonableness:** From the midpoint to the Planck length it is $-4 - (-35) = 31$ orders of magnitude and to the universe $27 - (-4) = 31$ orders of magnitude, so the gap is symmetric. The size $10^{-4}\,\text{m}$ is a tenth of a millimetre, about the thickness of a hair.

activities.title: How were the sizes found out?
activities.text:
No size in the simulation is the result of a single tape measure. Every size has been inferred from measurements and a model, and the method varies with the scale.

- **Proton**, $1.7\cdot10^{-15}\,\text{m}$: scattering of electrons from protons and measuring the energy levels of atoms.
- **Virus**, $1.0\cdot10^{-7}\,\text{m}$: the electron microscope.
- **Earth**, $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$: geodetic measurements and satellites.
- **Radius of Earth's orbit (1 AU)**, $1.5\cdot10^{11}\,\text{m}$: radar measurements of planets and probes.
- **Nearest star**, $4.0\cdot10^{16}\,\text{m}$: the apparent shift of the star as Earth orbits the Sun (parallax).
- **Universe**, $8.8\cdot10^{26}\,\text{m}$: observations of galaxies and a model of expansion.

question.prompt: A proton cannot be seen even with a powerful microscope. How, then, is its size known?

choices.text: Someone has measured the proton with a tiny tape measure, looking at it through a magnifying glass.
choices.feedback: No tape measure is this small, and a proton is not larger than the wavelength of light, so it cannot be seen with a magnifying glass. The size is inferred indirectly from experiments.

choices.text: In experiments, particles have been fired at protons and the way they scatter has been measured. From a model one calculates what size the proton must be for the scattering to look like this.
choices.feedback: Correct. The size is the combined result of measurements and a model: the measurement tells how the particles are deflected, and the model tells what the deflection means for the size. That is why refining the model can change the size.

choices.text: Physicists have agreed on the size by voting, because it cannot be measured.
choices.feedback: In physics, measurement decides the size, not a vote. Experiments are repeated in different laboratories, and results are accepted only when the methods give the same result.

choices.text: The size is calculated from theory alone, and no measurements are needed.
choices.feedback: Theory alone does not tell how large a proton is: measurement decides the size. Theory helps to interpret measurements, but its predictions are tested with experiments.

activities.title: Return to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with the readings of the simulation. How big is the difference between an atom and its nucleus, and how are the Solar System, the Milky Way and the observable universe related? Which difference in sizes surprised you most? Also return to the question at the start: from a proton to the observable universe there are about $27-(-15) = 42$ orders of magnitude, and from the Planck length about 62.

activities.title: Identify the object
activities.prompt: A radio telescope detects in the Milky Way an object from which a pulse of radiation comes steadily about 30 times a second. The mass of the object has been determined to be about $1.4$ solar masses, and according to other observations its diameter is only about $20\,\text{km}$. What object is it most likely to be?

choices.text: A star similar to the Sun.
choices.feedback: An ordinary star slightly more massive than the Sun would be of the size of the Sun, with a diameter of over a million kilometres, not $20\,\text{km}$. So large a mass in so small a space requires extremely dense matter.

The mass of a planet is much smaller than that of a star: even the largest planet, Jupiter, has only about a thousandth of the mass of the Sun. The mass of the object is greater than that of the Sun, so it cannot be a planet.

Correct. The mass is greater than that of the Sun but the diameter only about $20\,\text{km}$: the matter has been squeezed into almost pure neutrons. A neutron star can rotate tens of times a second, and its radiation beam sweeps past Earth once per rotation like the light of a lighthouse.

A black hole has no surface, and its size is the diameter of the event horizon. The known black holes formed as remnants of stars are about three solar masses or heavier, so an object of $1.4$ solar masses with a rotating surface $20\,\text{km}$ in size is a neutron star.

A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust whose size is light-years, that is, tens of trillions of kilometres, not $20\,\text{km}$. Stars can form in a nebula, but the nebula itself is not a compact object.

A galaxy is a system of billions of stars, gas and dust with a diameter of thousands or hundreds of thousands of light-years. The mass of a galaxy is billions of times the mass of the Sun, not $1.4$ times.

activities.title: Which interaction?
activities.prompt:
Which fundamental interaction explains each phenomenon?

1. A dropped bunch of keys falls to the floor.
2. A fridge magnet stays stuck to the fridge door.
3. The two protons and two neutrons of a helium nucleus stay together.
4. A banana contains a little radioactive potassium-40. Sometimes a neutron in its nucleus changes into a proton, and an electron leaves the nucleus.

choices.feedback: Correct. Earth and the keys attract each other because of gravity. The force between the magnet and the steel door is magnetic, that is, electromagnetic. The parts of the nucleus are held together by the residual effect of the strong interaction, and a neutron changing into a proton (beta decay) is caused by the weak interaction.

Gravity between the particles of a nucleus is far too weak: the electric repulsion of two protons is about $10^{36}$ times stronger than their gravity. The nucleus is held together by the residual effect of the strong interaction.

The electromagnetic interaction does not hold the nucleus together but tends to break it apart: protons have charges of the same sign and repel each other, and neutrons have no charge. The nucleus stays together because of the residual effect of the strong interaction.

As a whole, the bunch of keys and Earth are each almost electrically neutral, so there is no significant electric force between them. The fall is due to gravity, which acts between all masses and is always attractive.

In the decay of potassium-40 (beta decay) a neutron changes into a proton, that is, the kind of particle changes. A change like this is caused by the weak interaction. The strong interaction binds quarks and the parts of the nucleus together, but it does not change a neutron into a proton.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: Veera compares the Sun and Earth. The diameter of the Sun is $1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}$ and that of Earth $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$. She reasons: "The orders of magnitude are $10^{9}$ and $10^{7}$, so the difference is $9 - 7 = 2$. So the Sun is two times larger than Earth." Where is the error?

choices.text: The difference of orders of magnitude must not be calculated by subtraction.
choices.feedback: The difference is the right method: in dividing powers of ten the exponents are subtracted, and $9 - 7 = 2$ is correct. The error comes only from what the number 2 means.

choices.text: The difference $2$ is the number of powers of ten, so the Sun is about $10^{2} = 100$ times larger, not 2 times.
choices.feedback: Correct. Each order of magnitude is tenfold, so two orders of magnitude is a hundredfold difference. The exact ratio is $\dfrac{1.39\cdot10^{9}}{1.27\cdot10^{7}} \approx 109$.

choices.text: The diameter of Earth is actually larger than that of the Sun, so there is an error in the numbers.
choices.feedback: The numbers are correct: about a million Earths fit in the Sun. The error is not in the numbers but in how the difference of orders of magnitude is interpreted.

choices.text: The order of magnitude is $10^{9}$ only for the Sun; the order of magnitude of Earth cannot be determined.
choices.feedback: Both objects have an order of magnitude: the $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m}$ of Earth is of the order $10^{7}\,\text{m}$. The order of magnitude can be determined for every number.

activities.title: Optional: measuring the size of Earth
activities.prompt: Two surveyors stand on the same north–south line at a distance of $8.0\cdot10^{2}\,\text{km}$ from each other. At midday the Sun is directly overhead for one, but a vertical stick of the other surveyor casts a shadow showing that the Sun's ray is at an angle of $7.2^\circ$ to the stick. The Sun is so far away that its rays are parallel, so the angle $7.2^\circ$ is also the arc angle between the surveyors as seen from the centre of Earth. Earth is a sphere. What is the diameter of Earth? Answer in kilometres.
hints: Around the whole globe the arc angle is $360^\circ$. How many times does the angle $7.2^\circ$ fit in it?
The circumference is $C = \dfrac{360^\circ}{7.2^\circ}\cdot s$, where $s$ is the distance between the surveyors. The diameter is found from the circumference of a circle $C = \pi d$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the circumference $C$ of Earth. What was asked is the diameter, which is found by dividing the circumference by $\pi$.
This is the radius of Earth. The diameter is twice the radius, or the circumference divided by $\pi$.
This is the length of one degree on the surface of Earth, $\dfrac{800\,\text{km}}{7.2}$. The whole circumference has 360 degrees, and the diameter is found only from the circumference.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the distance between the surveyors $s = 8.0\cdot10^{2}\,\text{km}$ and the arc angle $\alpha = 7.2^\circ$; Earth is a sphere

**Find:** the diameter of Earth $d$ in kilometres

**Principle:** The distance between the surveyors is the same fraction of the circumference as the angle $7.2^\circ$ is of the whole turn $360^\circ$. The diameter is found from the circumference, because the circumference of a circle is $\pi$ times the diameter.

**Formula:** $\dfrac{s}{C} = \dfrac{\alpha}{360^\circ}$, so $C = \dfrac{360^\circ}{\alpha}\,s$, and $C = \pi d$, so $d = \dfrac{C}{\pi} = \dfrac{360^\circ\,s}{\pi\,\alpha}$

**Conversions:** Not needed: the distance is already in kilometres and the angles are in the same unit (degrees), so the angle units cancel.

**Substitution:** $d = \dfrac{360^\circ\cdot8.0\cdot10^{2}\,\text{km}}{\pi\cdot7.2^\circ} = \dfrac{4.0\cdot10^{4}\,\text{km}}{\pi} = 1.27\cdot10^{4}\,\text{km}$

**Answer:** $1.3\cdot10^{4}\,\text{km}$, that is, about $13\,000\,\text{km}$, two significant figures like the given measurements ($12\,700$ also fits in the field).

**Reasonableness:** The known diameter of Earth is $1.27\cdot10^{7}\,\text{m} = 1.27\cdot10^{4}\,\text{km}$, and the result agrees. The circumference $4.0\cdot10^{4}\,\text{km}$ is of the order $10^{4}\,\text{km}$, which corresponds to the size of the globe.

activities.text: Practise some more on three levels. Level 1 exercises use a single formula, and level 3 requires reasoning. Level 1 is enough for the basic skills; levels 2 and 3 are voluntary and deepen your understanding.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: The distance to Proxima Centauri is $4.0\cdot10^{16}\,\text{m}$. What is the order of magnitude of this distance?

choices.feedback: You ignored the factor part. When the factor part is more than about 3, the nearest power of ten is the next one: on the axis of powers of ten, the number $4.0\cdot10^{16}$ is closer to the point $10^{17}$ than to the point $10^{16}$.
Correct. The factor part $4.0$ is more than about 3, so the nearest power of ten is $10^{17}\,\text{m}$. The order of magnitude is always a power of ten with no factor.
This is the same number rounded, not an order of magnitude. The order of magnitude is a power of ten without a factor: $10^{n}$.
You picked the factor four as the exponent. The exponent is $16$, and the factor part $4.0$ only decides whether it rounds down or up.

activities.title: 2. Difference of orders of magnitude
activities.prompt: The order of magnitude of the size of object $\text{A}$ is $10^{3}\,\text{m}$ and that of object $\text{B}$ is $10^{8}\,\text{m}$. How many times larger is $\text{B}$, to the accuracy of an order of magnitude?

choices.feedback: You calculated the difference of the orders of magnitude, $8-3 = 5$, and read it as the ratio of the sizes. The difference 5 tells the number of steps of powers of ten, and each step is a tenfold size, so the ratio is $10^{5}$.

choices.text: About $10^{5}$, that is, a hundred thousand times larger
choices.feedback: Correct. Between the orders of magnitude there are $8-3 = 5$ steps, and each step is a tenfold size: $10\cdot10\cdot10\cdot10\cdot10 = 10^{5}$.
You added the exponents: $3+8 = 11$. The ratio of sizes is a division, and when powers of ten are divided, the exponents are subtracted: $10^{8}/10^{3} = 10^{8-3}$.
You divided the exponents by each other. The size is a power of ten, not an exponent: the ratio is $10^{8}/10^{3}$, and it is the difference of the exponents in the superscript, $10^{8-3} = 10^{5}$.

activities.title: 3. Calculation
activities.prompt: The diameter of the Sun is $1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of a neutron star is about $2.4\cdot10^{4}\,\text{m}$, although the mass of a neutron star is greater than that of the Sun. How many times larger is the diameter of the Sun than the diameter of the neutron star?
hints: The question "how many times larger" is a division: divide the larger size by the smaller.
The ratio of the sizes is $k = \dfrac{d_\text{Sun}}{d_\text{neutron star}}$.
$k = \dfrac{1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}}{2.4\cdot10^{4}\,\text{m}}$. Calculate with a calculator and check: the number of steps is $9-4 = 5$, so the answer should be close to $10^{5}$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the difference of the orders of magnitude, that is, the difference of the exponents, not the ratio of the sizes. The ratio is found by dividing the diameter of the Sun by the diameter of the neutron star.
You divided the smaller size by the larger. When asked how many times larger the Sun is, the diameter of the Sun is divided by the diameter of the neutron star.

activities.solution:
**Given:** the diameter of the Sun $d_\text{Sun} = 1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}$ and the diameter of the neutron star $d_\text{neutron star} = 2.4\cdot10^{4}\,\text{m}$

**Find:** the ratio of the sizes $k$ (how many times larger the diameter of the Sun is than the diameter of the neutron star)

**Principle:** The question "how many times larger" is a division: divide the larger size by the smaller.

**Formula:** $k = \dfrac{d_\text{Sun}}{d_\text{neutron star}}$

**Conversions:** Not needed: both diameters are in metres, so the unit cancels and $k$ is just a number.

**Substitution:** $k = \dfrac{1.39\cdot10^{9}\,\text{m}}{2.4\cdot10^{4}\,\text{m}} = 5.79\ldots\cdot10^{4}$

**Answer:** about $5.8\cdot10^{4}$, that is, $58\,000$ times; two significant figures, because the diameter of the neutron star $2.4\cdot10^{4}\,\text{m}$ is given with two.

**Reasonableness:** The orders of magnitude are $10^{9}\,\text{m}$ and $10^{4}\,\text{m}$. There are five steps of powers of ten between them, so the ratio should be about $10^{5}$, and $5.8\cdot10^{4}$ is close to that. So the neutron star is smaller than many a city, although its mass is greater than that of the Sun: size tells neither the type nor the mass of an object.

activities.title: 4. Explain
activities.prompt: Explain in your own words what the difference of orders of magnitude tells about the sizes of two objects, and why the simulation cannot show, for example, the Milky Way and an atom in the same picture in the right proportions of size. Use the words model, power of ten and order of magnitude.
criteria: I say that the difference of orders of magnitude is the number of steps of powers of ten and that each step is a tenfold size.
I say that a difference of 5 means a hundred-thousandfold difference, not a fivefold one.
I justify by calculation that the Milky Way ($10^{21}\,\text{m}$) and an atom ($10^{-10}\,\text{m}$) differ by about 31 orders of magnitude, so both cannot fit in the picture.
I say that the simulation is a model that shows one scale at a time and whose sizes are rounded.
activities.model: The difference of orders of magnitude tells how many steps of powers of ten the sizes of the objects are apart, and each step is a tenfold size. If the difference is five, the larger object is about $10^{5}$, that is, a hundred thousand times larger. The Milky Way is of the order $10^{21}\,\text{m}$ and a hydrogen atom $10^{-10}\,\text{m}$, so the difference is $21 - (-10) = 31$ orders of magnitude. If the Milky Way fills the picture, the size of the atom would be a fraction of a pixel, and the other way round. That is why the simulation is a model that draws the objects in the right proportions of size for only one scale at a time. The sizes of the model are rounded values, and their accuracy varies.

activities.text: Finally, two quick questions. Answer them yourself first, and only then open the answer.
